reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that sensory and imaginative processes are not mutually exclusive but operate within overlapping neural domains. The duality manifests in the intensity of cortical activation rather than spatial localization. In GSI, this translates into a Bayesian framework where sensory evidence and imagined priors are fused to compute posterior beliefs. The intensity parameter σ governs how strongly a cortical region responds, distinguishing hallucination from perception. In GSE, this becomes a state transition problem: given a sensory input, the system computes the likelihood of transitioning to an imagined state based on prior expectations. The boundary condition arises when mental interpretation M alters the perceived object O, causing P(O|M) ≠ P(O|S). This leads to a dualism in cognition—where perception is not just a passive reception but an active inference process shaped by intentionality. The failure mode occurs when σ drops below threshold θ, resulting in perceptual failure or hallucination. The epistemological implication is that reality is not fixed but emerges from the interaction of sensory data and internal models.

reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Two competing agents: the sensory agent (S) that receives external stimuli and the intentional agent (I) that generates internal predictions. Their interaction defines the perceptual space. When I dominates S, hallucination occurs; when S dominates I, perception prevails. The conflict is resolved through mutual information maximization in the cortical hierarchy.
